19	/// # Instruction Guidelines
20	///
21	/// We're inventing an instruction set here which naturally brings a whole set
22	/// of design questions. Note that this is explicitly intended to be only ever
23	/// used for Pulley where there are a different set of design constraints than
24	/// other instruction sets (e.g. general-purpose CPU ISAs). Some examples of
25	/// constraints for Pulley are:
26	///
27	/// * Instructions must be portable to many architectures.
28	/// * The Pulley ISA is mostly target-independent as the compilation target is
29	///   currently only parameterized on pointer width and endianness.
30	/// * Pulley instructions should be balance of time-to-decode and code size. For
31	///   example super fancy bit-packing tricks might be tough to decode in
32	///   software but might be worthwhile if it's quite common and greatly reduces
33	///   the size of bytecode. There's not a hard-and-fast answer here, but a
34	///   balance to be made.
35	/// * Many "macro ops" are present to reduce the size of compiled bytecode so
36	///   there is a wide set of duplicate functionality between opcodes (and this
37	///   is expected).
38	///
39	/// Given all this it's also useful to have a set of guidelines used to name and
40	/// develop Pulley instructions. As of the time of this writing it's still
41	/// pretty early days for Pulley so some of these guidelines may change over
42	/// time. Additionally instructions don't necessarily all follow these
43	/// conventions and that may also change over time. With that in mind, here's a
44	/// rough set of guidelines:
45	///
46	/// * Most instructions are prefixed with `x`, `f`, or `v`, indicating which
47	///   type of register they're operating on. (e.g. `xadd32` operates on the `x`
48	///   integer registers and `fadd32` operates on the `f` float registers).
49	///
50	/// * Most instructions are suffixed or otherwise contain the bit width they're
51	///   operating on. For example `xadd32` is a 32-bit addition.
52	///
53	/// * If an instruction operates on signed or unsigned data (such as division
54	///   and remainder), then the instruction is suffixed with `_s` or `_u`.
55	///
56	/// * Instructions operate on either 32 or 64-bit parts of a register.
57	///   Instructions modifying only 32-bits of a register always modify the "low"
58	///   part of a register and leave the upper part unmodified. This is intended
59	///   to help 32-bit platforms where if most operations are 32-bit there's no
60	///   need for extra instructions to sign or zero extend and modify the upper
61	///   half of the register.
62	///
63	/// * Binops use `BinaryOperands<T>` for the destination and argument registers.
64	///
65	/// * Instructions operating on memory contain a few pieces of information:

70	///   │  │  │ │  │     ▼
71	///   │  │  │ │  │     addressing mode
72	///   │  │  │ │  ▼
73	///   │  │  │ │  width of register modified + sign-extension (optional)
74	///   │  │  │ ▼
75	///   │  │  │ endianness of the operation (le/be)
76	///   │  │  ▼
77	///   │  │  bit-width of the operation
78	///   │  ▼
79	///   │  what's happening (load/store)

The implementation is complete. Here's a summary of what I did:

## Changes

The Pulley instruction set is entirely macro-driven from two lists in `pulley/src/lib.rs`. `op.rs`, `encode.rs`, `decode.rs`, `opcode.rs`, and `disas.rs` all generate their code from `for_each_op!` / `for_each_extended_op!`, so the reorganization is driven by moving entries between those two macros. Only `interp.rs` (hand-written visitor impls) needed manual method relocation.

**`pulley/src/lib.rs`** — Moved three instructions from `for_each_op!` to `for_each_extended_op!`:
- `xadd64_uoverflow_trap = Xadd64UoverflowTrap { operands: BinaryOperands<XReg> }`
- `xpush32_many = XPush32Many { srcs: RegSet<XReg> }`
- `xpop32_many = XPop32Many { dsts: RegSet<XReg> }`

This automatically regenerates:
- `op.rs`: these become `ExtendedOp` variants; their `From<T> for Op` now produces `Op::ExtendedOp(ExtendedOp::T(...))`.
- `encode.rs`: they now use the extended encoder (`WIDTH = 3 + fields` instead of `1 + fields`), consuming the extra byte for the two-byte extended opcode prefix — which shifts all subsequent disassembly byte offsets.
- `decode.rs` / `opcode.rs`: they decode via the extended-opcode path.

**`pulley/src/interp.rs`** — Moved the hand-written `xadd64_uoverflow_trap`, `xpush32_many`, and `xpop32_many` method bodies out of the `OpVisitor for Interpreter` impl and into the `ExtendedOpVisitor for Interpreter` impl (bodies unchanged).

**`pulley/src/regs.rs`** — Added manual `PartialOrd`, `Ord`, and `Hash` impls for `RegSet<R>`. The `ExtendedOp` structs derive these traits (regular `Op` structs don't), and since `XPush32Many`/`XPop32Many` carry a `RegSet<XReg>` field, `RegSet` now needs them. I used manual impls (matching the existing manual `PartialEq`/`Eq`) delegating to the underlying bitset storage so no bound on `R` is required.

## Verification
- `pulley-interpreter` builds with `--all-features` and with the encode/decode/disas/interp features.
- `cranelift-codegen` (which consumes the macros to generate its Pulley backend) builds — the meta generator chains both op lists and already skips the `*_many` ops, and `xadd64_uoverflow_trap` still resolves to the same `encode::xadd64_uoverflow_trap` function name.

I left the `tests/` directory untouched, as instructed. The existing `tests/all/disas.rs` still references `Op::XPush32Many(...)` directly and expects the old byte offsets; those will be corrected by the verification system's test patch.
